Series::cplxpair¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::cplxpair() const

Put Conjugate Roots Next To Each Other¶

cplxpair() reorganizes a series whose non-real values occur in complex- conjugate pairs. Each pair is made adjacent, the member with negative imaginary part comes first, and pairs are ordered by real part and then by imaginary magnitude. Values with zero imaginary part follow all conjugate pairs in ascending real order.

This is useful after a polynomial-root or eigenvalue calculation when a real problem produces conjugate roots but does not promise a presentation order. The method turns that unordered result into a deterministic layout without discarding either component of a complex value.

Pairing is global, not axis-local. The receiver is read in logical flattened order, reordered once, and reshaped to the original dimensions. Consequently, the original shape is metadata retained around one ordered sequence; rows or planes are not paired independently.

For floating roundoff, two values qualify as conjugates when their real parts and opposite imaginary parts agree within a scale-aware tolerance of 100 * epsilon * max(1, abs(a), abs(b)). A tiny imaginary component within that tolerance is treated as zero. Every non-real value must still have one unused partner. An unmatched value is rejected rather than silently moved into the real tail.

For a real-valued receiver there is nothing to pair. cplxpair() therefore performs one global ascending sort and restores the original shape. Complex input retains its complex dtype; real input retains its dtype. The result is an out-of-place, contiguous series on the receiver’s platform.

Reverse Mode¶

The operation changes positions, not values. Reverse mode applies the inverse permutation to the incoming sensitivity, so each source element receives the sensitivity attached to its ordered destination. Pair discovery itself is discrete: gradients describe the selected ordering and do not differentiate through a change in which two values qualify as partners.

Examples¶

Example 1. Conjugate pairs come first; real values form the sorted tail.

using Complex = std::complex<double>;
auto roots = pluss::make_series(std::vector<Complex>{
    {3.0, 0.0}, {2.0, 4.0}, {1.0, -2.0}, {2.0, -4.0},
    {-1.0, 0.0}, {1.0, 2.0}}, {6});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, roots.cplxpair());

Output¶

Series(shape=[6], strides=[1], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[(1.0000-2.0000j), (1.0000+2.0000j), (2.0000-4.0000j), (2.0000+4.0000j), (-1.0000+0.0000j), (3.0000+0.0000j)]

Example 2. A real matrix is sorted globally, not one row at a time.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({{4, 1, 3}, {0, -2, 8}}).cplxpair());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -2 0 1 ⎤
⎣  3 4 8 ⎦

Example 3. Higher-rank shape is retained even though pairing is global.

using Complex = std::complex<double>;
auto paired = pluss::make_series(std::vector<Complex>{
    {2.0, 1.0}, {2.0, -1.0}, {1.0, 3.0}, {1.0, -3.0}}, {2, 2})
                  .cplxpair();
std::cout << "dtype=" << paired.scalar_type()
          << " dim=" << paired.dim()
          << " shape=[" << paired.size(0) << ',' << paired.size(1) << ']';

Output¶

dtype=complex128 dim=2 shape=[2,2]

Example 4. Weighted reverse mode reveals the inverse permutation. The original first element moves to the fourth output position, so it receives weight four.

using Complex = std::complex<double>;
auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<Complex>{
    {2.0, 1.0}, {1.0, -3.0}, {2.0, -1.0}, {1.0, 3.0}}, {4});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.cplxpair()
 .real()
 .mul(pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0}))
 .sum()
 .reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=complex128, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[(4.0000+0.0000j), (1.0000+0.0000j), (3.0000+0.0000j), (2.0000+0.0000j)]

Example 5. An unmatched non-real value is a contract error.

using Complex = std::complex<double>;
try {
  (void)pluss::make_series(
      std::vector<Complex>{{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 0.0}}, {2}).cplxpair();
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  const std::string message = e.what();
  std::cout << message.substr(0, message.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

cplxpair: complex value has no conjugate partner
